Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.

Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.

Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

But doctors stress it is a long way from knowing how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.

Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.

The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.

"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.

Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.

Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.

Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.

The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.

Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.

tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients

just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear

for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans

Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US . It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS , external , found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

There are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease in Britain each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include , external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

MN202611_1s8jxmqcu3k.t:
Sweden was among countries to report a cyber incident in which some supermarket fridge units had been hiked up in temperature

A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies .

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pentest Partners who helped raise the alarm.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.

They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.

Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely, or in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.

BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.

"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did want to be publicly named.

"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.

There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:

In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted

On 11th and 12th October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted

On the 1st and 2nd of November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted

The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).

RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.

As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.

These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.

Each RDM controller can be used to remotely control the temperature of dozens of fridges and freezers

"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.

"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.

RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.

The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.

"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.

He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included, dismantling our hardware".

"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.

RDM confirmed that there is no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continues to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.

If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

Hospital doctors also took strike action in June 2026

Resident doctors are set to return to the picket lines on Friday in a strike over pay.

They will hold a full 24-hour strike starting at 07:00 GMT, marking their second such action this year .

British Medical Association (BMA) members voted in favour of industrial action after the union rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise from an independent pay body.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said he remained committed to delivering the pay award and that he would "do everything in my power" to implement it this year - but said he was unable to do so in the absence of a Stormont budget .

Dr Steven Montgomery, the chairman of the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said doctors should not have to strike for a second time but the issues that had originally taken them to the picket lines remained unresolved.

"Our pay is eroding and we need to address that in order to retain young doctors in Northern Ireland," he said.

Hospital doctors to strike as pay dispute continues

Health workers run out of patience with Stormont budget delay

Healthcare workers at 'tipping point' as union ballots for industrial action

Resident doctors are fully qualified medical practitioners who are completing postgraduate clinical training in a hospital or general practice under the supervision of a senior doctor.

Consultants and specialist, associate specialist and speciality grade (SAS) doctors will also take 24-hour action from 07:00 GMT on Monday.

They will provide what is known as Christmas Day cover, which means that most routine and elective services will be cancelled but full emergency cover will remain in place.

SAS doctors are specialist doctors employed by health trusts.

The three branches of hospital doctors also took strike action in June .

During this period of strike action more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled across the health and social care system, according to the health minister.

Steven Montgomery says doctors face burnout due to pressure on them at work

Butler said the fresh action planned for Friday and Monday would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery", especially during the busy winter period.

In England, consultant doctors have called off their two-day strike this month to hold talks with the government.

Montgomery said colleagues wanted the best for the health service and their patients but were facing burnout and emotional distress due to work pressure, with their pay failing to reflect the demands placed upon them.

He said doctors wanted full "pay restoration", adding that the annual pay rise they were due to receive would not make up for the value their pay had lost over many years.

Montgomery added that the BMA was "more than willing" to discuss with the minister and Department of Health how pay "erosion" could be addressed and what steps were needed to reassure members that there was a commitment to resolving it.

The BMA balloted its members over a four-week period

Butler said the recommended 3.5% rise was higher than that for other healthcare professionals working in Northern Ireland's health system.

He added that to go beyond the recommended offer would lead to "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

"It comes on top of an average cumulative pay uplifts over the last three years of 30% for resident doctors, 25% for speciality, associate specialist, and specialist doctors, and 24% for consultants," he said.

The minister said he had met the BMA and outlined the financial constraints facing the Department of Health and his intention to issue the pay rises as soon as possible.

But he said that would require adequate funding to be given to his department.
